title: Tool Use, MCP & Streaming
scopeHtml: Scope: the tool-use loop and block pairing rules, schema design, MCP transports and connector, and safe handling of streamed responses.

notes.title: The tool-use loop
notes.html:
The most common misconception. People think Claude runs tools. It does not. Claude reads your tool definitions, decides one fits the situation, and tells your application what to call and with which inputs. Your application executes the tool, gets the result, and sends it back; then Claude continues. The boundary between what Claude owns and what your code owns is where most tool-use bugs live.

The six steps.

  1. Define the tools: name, description, input_schema. Claude reads these to decide whether and when to call a tool.
  2. Send a message that includes the tool definitions and the user's input.
  3. Claude returns a tool_use block containing the tool name, a unique ID and the input arguments. The response has stop_reason: tool_use.
  4. Your code executes the tool. By now the assistant turn has ended; Claude is not holding a connection open or waiting on your server. The model is stateless between calls, so to continue you make a fresh request containing the prior messages plus the tool result.
  5. Return a tool_result block that references the original tool-use ID.
  6. Claude continues, either with another tool_use block (loop again) or a final answer with stop_reason: end_turn.

Skeleton of a correct loop.

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_input}]
for _ in range(MAX_ITERATIONS):                      # exit condition not left to Claude
    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages, max_tokens=2048)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})   # keep ALL blocks
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    results = []
    for block in resp.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":
            try:
                out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": out})
            except Exception as e:
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                                "is_error": True, "content": f"Tool failed: {e}"})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

Key facts.

  • The loop is not automatic; step 4 is yours.
  • Define your own iteration cap and other exit conditions.
  • Check stop_reason before continuing: only tool_use means tool calls are ready to run.
  • If a miss is systematic (wrong tool, wrong args), the fix is usually in the schema definition step.

Real life. A restaurant: the waiter (Claude) writes the order; the kitchen (your code) cooks it; the dish goes back to the table. The waiter does not cook, and the table gets nothing if the kitchen never returns the dish.

Tech. An RPC client that serializes the call; the server (your function) executes and replies.

notes.title: Block pairing rules
notes.html:
Messages are lists of typed blocks, not plain text. Four block types do the work in a tool-use session:

Block From Contains Critical rule
text Claude prose May appear beside a tool_use in the same turn. Preserve the full content array, including the text block, when appending to history; dropping it corrupts context.
tool_use Claude tool name, unique ID, input arguments Every one must be answered by a tool_result with the same ID in the immediately following user turn.
tool_result You (user turn) matching tool_use_id, content, optional is_error: true The ID must match exactly; it is how Claude connects each result to its call, which matters for multiple or out-of-order results.
thinking Claude (extended thinking only) internal reasoning Pass back unchanged (signature). Redacted thinking too.

The invariant. Every tool_use in an assistant turn must have a corresponding tool_result in the immediately following user turn. A missing result, an ID mismatch, a result placed in a later turn, or turns out of order fails validation. This is structural, not something you can repair by adjusting the prompt; your code must produce the sequence correctly on every request.

Multiple calls in one turn. Claude can issue several tool_use blocks (parallel calls). Resolve all of them together in the next user turn. Results can be in any order because IDs link them.

Failures. A tool that fails still gets a tool_result, with is_error: true and a useful message. Returning nothing, or an empty success, leaves Claude to reason on a false premise.

Real life. Every library book borrowed must be matched by a return slip with the same card number before the next loan. A slip delivered two days later, or with the wrong number, is rejected.

Tech. Request/response correlation IDs in async messaging.

Common mistakes. Returning only the successful results of parallel calls; dropping the text block from history; letting a streamed partial turn into history (see streaming).

notes.title: Writing tool schemas
notes.html:
A tool has three parts: name, description, input_schema (JSON Schema). Claude chooses a tool almost entirely from the description plus the name, with parameter types as a secondary signal.

Name. Short and specific: get_account_balance beats get_data.

Description (the routing mechanism). Write 3 to 4 sentences covering what it does, when to use it and when not to, and what it returns; include sample inputs where format matters.

  • "Use this to find information" fails: Claude cannot tell it from any other retrieval tool.
  • "Use this to retrieve the current balance for a specific account ID; do not use for transaction history" gives an exclusion condition Claude can reason with.
  • Too short: Claude guesses. Too long: the trigger conditions get buried.

Input schema decisions.

Decision Guidance Why
Required fields Mark required only when the call is meaningless without it (place in required) Marking everything required forces Claude to fabricate values it has no basis for
Optional fields For parameters with sensible defaults or where absence carries meaning; give defaults in the function Lets Claude omit what it does not know
Overlapping tools/parameters Add disambiguating language to each tool's description naming its domain or trigger With identical signatures, routing collapses to description alone
Dependencies between calls Dependent calls run in separate turns; independent calls can be issued together (current models default to parallel) A dependent call can't be built until the first result exists
Parallelism control disable_parallel_tool_use forces one call per turn When you need strict sequencing

Worked failure and fix. Two tools, search_docs ("Use this to find information about the product") and get_context_summary ("Use this to retrieve relevant information from the current session"), caused Claude to call search_docs when the answer was already in context. Fix: add an exclusion to both: search_docs: "…when the question requires content not already present in this conversation. Do not call if the answer is in the current session." and get_context_summary: "Only use if the answer is already present in the session. Do not use to look up new information." One sentence to say when, one to say when not. If descriptions still cannot be cleanly separated, merge the tools into one with a type parameter.

Caveat. Exclusion rules that depend on earlier turns silently fail if history is truncated, because Claude can no longer see those turns.

Over-tooling. Every extra tool enlarges the surface Claude must reason over. Teams register everything "just in case" and selection quality degrades. Start with the minimum set; add a tool only for a confirmed capability gap. (Under-tooling is the opposite failure: the agent hallucinates a path.)

Real life. Two light switches both labelled "lights". Add "hallway only" and "everything except the hallway" and nobody guesses wrong.

Tech. Two REST endpoints with identical docs: clients call the wrong one until the docs say when each applies.

notes.title: MCP
notes.html:
What it is. The Model Context Protocol is a standardized layer that moves tool definitions and execution out of your application and into dedicated servers. When a maintained server exists for a service (GitHub is the standard example), you connect to it instead of writing a schema and execution function for every operation and maintaining them as the service's API evolves.

How it fits the loop. The loop does not change. Your MCP client sends a ListToolsRequest, receives the tool list, and passes those definitions to Claude. Claude still emits tool_use, your application still executes and returns tool_result, and the pairing rules still apply. From Claude's perspective MCP tools are indistinguishable from ones you authored. What changes is who wrote and who owns the definitions. MCP servers can also expose resources and prompts, not only tools.

Transports.

  • stdio: local servers; your application spawns the server as a subprocess and talks over standard input/output.
  • Streamable HTTP: remote servers over the network; POST for client→server messages plus an optional GET-based SSE stream for server-initiated messages.
  • An older SSE-only transport is deprecated; new integrations use Streamable HTTP.

The API MCP Connector. Lets the Messages API connect to MCP servers for you.

  • Supports remote (HTTP) servers only. A stdio server needs a client you manage yourself (SDK) or Claude Desktop / Claude Code.
  • Requires the beta header mcp-client-2025-11-20; without it the mcp_toolset configuration does not apply as described.
  • Control via an mcp_toolset object in the tools array: default_config (applies to every tool on the server), per-tool overrides in configs keyed by tool name, enabled (turn individual tools on/off: allowlist/denylist), and defer_loading (delay loading a tool definition until needed, cutting upfront context cost for servers with large tool lists).

Context cost. MCP servers add tool definitions to the context window even when the tools are not used in the current turn. Connect only the servers you are actively using; check the budget when connecting several.

When to use what.

  • Use MCP when a well-maintained server covers the operations you need.
  • Write schemas yourself when no server fits, or you need precise control over description quality (scope can often be handled by the connector's allow/deny lists).
  • Use both: server for breadth, your tuned descriptions and allowlisting for the few tools you route to.

Real life. USB-C: any laptop talks to any charger or monitor because the port is standard; you do not custom-wire each device.

Tech. The Language Server Protocol: one protocol, many editors and language servers.

notes.title: Streaming
notes.html:
What changes. A non-streamed call returns one complete message. A streamed call sends a series of events describing the message as it is built; your code reassembles it. The final message is identical to a non-streamed one, but you assemble the pieces and decide what to do if the events stop early. Each event is a small independent message about one change; the model is not holding a live object open for you.

The event sequence.

Event Signals Your handler
message_start new message begins (shell with empty content, initial usage) create an empty content array
content_block_start a block opens (type: text/tool_use/thinking, and index) create a slot at that index; a tool_use block opens with name and id but no input yet
content_block_delta incremental piece of one block append the fragment: text fragment, thinking fragment, or input_json_delta (a partial JSON string)
content_block_stop the block at this index is complete finalize; first moment tool JSON is complete enough to parse
message_delta top-level changes: stop_reason, final usage record the stop reason
message_stop stream complete the assembled content is the finished message

The rules that prevent corrupted state.

  1. Never act on a partial block. Tool input arrives as partial JSON spread over many deltas; it is not valid until content_block_stop. Parse or execute before that and you get malformed JSON or half the arguments.
  2. Commit the assistant turn to history only after message_stop, with every block fully assembled.
  3. Interrupted stream: discard the partial assistant turn, then retry from the last complete turn. A half-built tool_use in history makes the next request fail validation.
  4. Check stop_reason from message_delta before continuing a loop: tool_use means calls are ready; anything else is a different path.

The incident to remember. A handler appended the assistant turn when its read loop ended. A network blip ended one stream after a tool_use block opened and received part of its JSON. The read loop ended as always, the handler stored a turn with truncated JSON, and the retry failed validation. The team audited the schema and retry logic for an afternoon; the cause was upstream. A stream ending is not the same as a message completing.

Real life. Watching a download. A half-downloaded file looks like a file but will not open; you only trust it at 100%.

Tech. TCP reassembly: a connection that dropped mid-message must not be treated as a delivered message.

When to stream. Long responses and user-facing interfaces. For short responses and backend jobs, a non-streamed call is simpler and removes the partial-state risk. For tool calls under streaming, accumulate deltas by index and reconstruct the calls from completed blocks.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
The loop. Claude requests, your code executes. Stateless between calls: resend prior messages plus the result. Loop on stop_reason: tool_use; stop on end_turn; add your own iteration cap and exit conditions. Systematic misses usually point to the schema.

Pairing. Blocks: text, tool_use, tool_result, thinking. Every tool_use needs a tool_result with the same ID in the immediately following user turn; resolve parallel calls together; failures return is_error: true; keep the full content array; return thinking unchanged. Violations fail validation and are not promptable.

Schemas. Specific name; description says what, when, when not, and what it returns (3 to 4 sentences); required only when essential; optional with defaults; exclusions on both overlapping tools or merge them; history truncation breaks exclusions; minimum tool set; disable_parallel_tool_use when needed.

MCP. Servers own definitions and execution; loop unchanged (ListToolsRequest). Transports: stdio (local), Streamable HTTP (remote), SSE-only deprecated. API connector: remote only, beta header mcp-client-2025-11-20, mcp_toolset with default_config, configs, enabled, defer_loading. Definitions cost context even if unused. Combine MCP breadth with tuned descriptions.

Streaming. Reassemble events (message_start … message_stop). Tool input is partial JSON until content_block_stop. Commit the turn only after message_stop; discard partial turns on interruption; check stop_reason. A finished read loop is not a finished message.

One-liners.

  • "Claude asks; your code acts."
  • "Every tool_use gets a tool_result, same ID, next turn."
  • "Tell Claude when not to use the tool."
  • "A stream that ended is not a message that completed."

questions.promptHtml:
Who executes a tool when Claude decides to use it?

  • A. Claude runs the function inside the API and returns the result
  • B. Your application: Claude returns a tool_use block, your code runs the tool and sends back a tool_result in a new request
  • C. Anthropic's servers always run it in a sandbox
  • D. The SDK runs it automatically with no code from you

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Claude only requests the call. The model is stateless between calls, so you make a fresh request with the prior messages plus the result.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The response has stop_reason: tool_use. The loop is not automatic: step four (execute) is yours. Server-run tools (like code execution) and Managed Agents are different paths, but for client-defined tools your code owns execution. Most tool bugs live on this boundary.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking Claude "waits" on an open connection for the result.
  • Forgetting to loop until stop_reason is end_turn.

questions.promptHtml:
In one assistant turn Claude emits three tool_use blocks. Your code returns two tool_result blocks in the next user turn and the third in a later turn. What happens?

  • A. The API accepts it and Claude waits for the third
  • B. The request fails validation: every tool_use must be answered by a tool_result with the same ID in the immediately following user turn
  • C. The third tool call is silently dropped
  • D. Claude re-issues the third call automatically

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. All tool_use blocks from one assistant turn must be resolved together, in the next user turn, with matching IDs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: This is structural, not promptable. Results can arrive out of order because the ID, not position, links each result to its call. If one tool fails, still return a tool_result for it with is_error: true.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running parallel calls and returning only the successful ones.
  • Dropping the text block that arrived with the tool_use when appending to history.

questions.contextHtml: A developer registers search_docs ("Use this to find information about the product") and get_context_summary ("Use this to retrieve relevant information from the current session"). Claude often calls search_docs when the answer is already in the conversation. They have re-run the test four times.
questions.promptHtml:
What is the most effective fix?

  • A. Rename the tools to longer names
  • B. Add an exclusion to both descriptions: when to use each and when not to (e.g. "Do not call if the answer is already in the current session")
  • C. Add "please choose carefully" to the system prompt
  • D. Mark every parameter required

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Renaming the tools or telling Claude to be careful. The two descriptions are indistinguishable at decision time, so wording elsewhere will not help.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the exact descriptions? Is full history sent every request (exclusion logic relies on it)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Patch both descriptions with a use-when and a do-not-use-when sentence.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Overlapping descriptions; truncated history; too many registered tools.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the failing prompts with traces of which tool was chosen.
  5. Root cause: Both descriptions say "find information"; routing collapses to description alone.
  6. Fix: B. If the descriptions still cannot be separated, merge into one tool with a type parameter.
  7. Prevention: An eval set of boundary-case inputs for tool selection.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on names alone; not stuff long essays into descriptions, which bury the trigger.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • What if history is truncated to save tokens? → The exclusion rule silently fails because Claude can no longer see prior turns.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the model.
  • Hire: adds exclusion conditions.
  • Strong hire: adds exclusions to both, notes the history dependency, proposes a boundary-case eval and the merge option.

questions.promptHtml:
A tool has ten parameters and the author marked all of them required "to be safe". What is the likely production effect?

  • A. Claude refuses to call the tool
  • B. Claude fabricates values for fields it has no basis to fill in
  • C. Claude calls the tool less often but with better inputs
  • D. None; required is only documentation

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Required means "non-negotiable", so Claude invents values to satisfy it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Mark a field required only when the call makes no sense without it. Fields with defaults or meaningful absence stay optional so Claude can omit what it does not know. Related: too many tools with overlapping parameters degrade routing, so start with the minimum tool set.

questions.promptHtml:
You want to attach a local filesystem MCP server (stdio) directly to a Messages API request through the MCP connector. What is true?

  • A. The connector supports stdio servers natively
  • B. The connector supports only remote HTTP servers; a stdio server needs you (or Claude Desktop/Claude Code) to act as the MCP client
  • C. Stdio servers are required for remote services
  • D. SSE-only is the recommended transport for new integrations

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Local servers use stdio (subprocess); remote servers use Streamable HTTP; the API MCP connector handles only the remote kind.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Streamable HTTP uses POST for client→server messages plus an optional GET-based SSE stream; SSE-only is deprecated (D). The connector requires the mcp-client-2025-11-20 beta header and an mcp_toolset entry in tools, where default_config, per-tool configs, enabled (allow/deny) and defer_loading (load definitions on demand) control scope and context cost. Tool definitions cost context even when unused.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Connecting many servers and burning the window before the first message.
  • Forgetting the beta header, so mcp_toolset settings do not apply.

questions.contextHtml: A streaming agent appends the assistant turn to history when its read loop exits. On a network blip, a stream ends after a tool_use block opened and received part of its JSON but before content_block_stop. The user retries; the retry fails with a validation error pointing at a malformed tool_use block. The team spends an afternoon auditing the tool schema.
questions.promptHtml:
What is the root cause and fix?

  • A. The tool schema is invalid; rewrite it
  • B. "The read loop ended" was treated as "the message is complete"; only message_stop means whole, so gate the history append on it, discard the partial turn and retry from the last complete turn
  • C. Switch to non-streaming permanently
  • D. Parse the partial JSON optimistically and run the tool

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Debugging the schema or retry logic because the error surfaces on the retry request, not the failed stream.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the previous turn built from a stream? Did it end with message_stop?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop the half-built assistant turn from stored history.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Partial block committed; schema bug; ID mismatch.
  4. How I'd verify each: Inspect the stored turn for truncated input JSON.
  5. Root cause: B.
  6. Fix: Accumulate input_json_delta by block index, parse only after content_block_stop, commit the turn after message_stop, check stop_reason before continuing.
  7. Prevention: A fault-injection test that cuts the stream mid-block.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not abandon streaming; it is right for user-facing output.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Is a partial text block as dangerous? → Cosmetic for display, but still do not store it as a complete turn.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rewrites the schema.
  • Hire: identifies the partial block.
  • Strong hire: gates on message_stop, discards and retries, adds fault-injection tests.

questions.promptHtml:
After Claude returns a tool_use block, what must your next request contain?

  • A. Only the tool result
  • B. The prior messages plus a tool_result for that call
  • C. Nothing; Claude keeps the session open
  • D. A new system prompt

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The model is stateless between calls, so you resend the conversation plus the result.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The assistant turn has already ended; Claude is not holding a connection open. Sending only the result (A) loses the context that made the call meaningful.

questions.promptHtml:
Your loop should continue only when which condition holds?

  • A. The response contains any text
  • B. stop_reason is tool_use; it ends on end_turn
  • C. The response is longer than 100 tokens
  • D. Always continue until a timeout

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. tool_use means your tool calls are ready to run; other values are different paths.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Add your own exit conditions (max iterations) so the loop does not depend on Claude volunteering to stop.

questions.promptHtml:
Two independent lookups are needed, and a third call depends on both results. How should this run?

  • A. All three in one turn
  • B. The two independent calls in one turn (parallel), the dependent call in a later turn
  • C. Three separate turns always
  • D. The dependent call first

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Dependent calls need earlier results, so they go in separate turns.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Current models default to parallel calls when independent. disable_parallel_tool_use forces one call per turn if you need it.

questions.promptHtml:
Which description is best for a balance lookup tool?

  • A. "Use this to find information."
  • B. "Retrieves the current balance for one account ID. Do not use for transaction history. Returns amount and currency."
  • C. "Gets data."
  • D. "Account tool."

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. It says what it does, an exclusion, and what it returns.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Too short and Claude guesses; too long and the trigger is buried. Aim for 3 to 4 sentences with example inputs where format matters.

questions.promptHtml:
Two tools are so similar that even long exclusions cannot separate them. What is the best structural fix?

  • A. Add more exclusions forever
  • B. Merge them into one tool with a type parameter
  • C. Rename both
  • D. Raise the temperature

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. If descriptions cannot be cleanly separated, they are one tool.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Every extra tool increases the surface Claude must reason over, so over-tooling degrades routing.

questions.promptHtml:
Three parallel tool calls finish out of order. How does Claude match results to calls?

  • A. By position in the list
  • B. By tool_use_id
  • C. By tool name
  • D. By timestamp

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The ID, not order or name, links each result to its call.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Two calls to the same tool would be ambiguous by name. Return all results in the immediately following user turn.

questions.promptHtml:
Five MCP servers are connected, but a task uses one. What is the side effect?

  • A. None
  • B. All tool definitions occupy context even when unused
  • C. Claude calls every tool
  • D. The servers disconnect

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Register only what you use; defer_loading and enabled reduce the cost.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: In the API connector these live in mcp_toolset (default_config, per-tool configs). The connector needs the mcp-client-2025-11-20 beta header.

questions.promptHtml:
A well-maintained GitHub MCP server exists. You need broad coverage but precise routing on three tools. Best approach?

  • A. Hand-write every GitHub schema
  • B. Connect the MCP server for breadth, allowlist the needed tools, and tune those tools' descriptions
  • C. Avoid MCP
  • D. Connect and expose everything

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Use both: breadth from the server, precision from allowlisting and description tuning.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Narrowing the tool set and sharpening descriptions are separate levers; use both.

questions.promptHtml:
When is it safe to parse a streamed tool call's input JSON?

  • A. After the first content_block_delta
  • B. After content_block_stop for that block
  • C. After message_start
  • D. Never

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Tool input arrives as partial JSON across deltas and is only complete once the block closes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Commit the whole assistant turn to history only after message_stop, and check stop_reason from message_delta before continuing.

questions.promptHtml:
A stream drops mid-response. What should you do?

  • A. Save the partial turn and continue
  • B. Discard the partial assistant turn and retry from the last complete turn
  • C. Parse whatever JSON you have
  • D. Switch to a smaller model

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. A half-built turn in history corrupts the next request.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Track completion explicitly: a turn is usable only once message_stop has arrived. A dropped stream is a transient failure, so retry the whole request.
